prompt: Which enantiomer of glyceraldehyde occurs naturally?

choices.text: The R enantiomer, which rotates plane-polarized light clockwise (+)
The S enantiomer, which rotates plane-polarized light counterclockwise (−)
choices.why: That is L-glyceraldehyde. Only the dextrorotatory enantiomer occurs naturally.

choices.text: The R enantiomer, which rotates plane-polarized light counterclockwise (−)
choices.why: The R enantiomer is dextrorotatory, (+), not levorotatory.

choices.text: Both enantiomers, as a 1 : 1 mixture
choices.why: Only the dextrorotatory enantiomer occurs naturally.

explanation: Only the dextrorotatory enantiomer of glyceraldehyde occurs naturally; it rotates plane-polarized light clockwise, (+), and has R configuration at carbon 2. (R)-(+)-glyceraldehyde is also called D-glyceraldehyde; the other enantiomer, the levorotatory (S) form, is L-glyceraldehyde.

prompt: What makes a monosaccharide a D sugar?

choices.text: R configuration at the chirality center farthest from the carbonyl group
It rotates plane-polarized light clockwise, like D-glyceraldehyde
choices.why: D and L have no relation to the direction of rotation; a D sugar can be dextrorotatory or levorotatory.

choices.text: All of its –OH groups point to the right in a Fischer projection
choices.why: Only the –OH at the lowest chirality center has to point to the right.

choices.text: R configuration at the chirality center nearest the carbonyl group
choices.why: The deciding center is the one farthest from the carbonyl group.

explanation: D sugars have the same R configuration as D-glyceraldehyde at the chirality center farthest from the carbonyl group. In Fischer projections, the –OH at that bottom chirality center points to the right.

prompt: An aldohexose is (2R,3S,4R,5R)-2,3,4,5,6-pentahydroxyhexanal. Is it a D sugar or an L sugar?

choices.text: D, because carbon 5, the lowest chirality center, is R
L, because carbon 3, a chirality center in the middle, is S
choices.why: D or L depends only on the lowest chirality center, carbon 5, which is R.

choices.text: It can't be told without measuring its optical rotation
choices.why: D and L have no relation to the direction of rotation. They are decided by the configuration at the lowest chirality center.

choices.text: It can't be told without the configuration at carbon 6
choices.why: Carbon 6 is a –CH2OH group, not a chirality center. The lowest chirality center is carbon 5.

explanation: In a hexanal, carbon 1 is the aldehyde carbon and carbon 6 is –CH2OH, so the chirality center farthest from the carbonyl is carbon 5. It is R, the same configuration as D-glyceraldehyde, so this is a D sugar.

prompt: (+)-Arabinose, an aldopentose, is (2R,3S,4S)-2,3,4,5-tetrahydroxypentanal. Is it a D sugar or an L sugar?

choices.text: An L sugar, because carbon 4 is S
A D sugar, because it is dextrorotatory
choices.why: The (+) sign has nothing to do with D or L; only the configuration at the lowest chirality center matters.

choices.text: A D sugar, because carbon 2 is R
choices.why: Carbon 2 is next to the carbonyl. The deciding center is the one farthest from it, carbon 4.

choices.text: Neither, because the D,L system applies only to aldohexoses
choices.why: The D,L system applies to monosaccharides in general, including glyceraldehyde and aldopentoses.

explanation: Carbon 5 of this pentanal is –CH2OH, so carbon 4 is the chirality center farthest from the carbonyl. It is S, so (+)-arabinose is an L sugar (Exercise 25.3.2), even though it is dextrorotatory.

prompt: What does the D in a sugar's name tell you about the direction in which it rotates plane-polarized light?

choices.text: Nothing; a D sugar can be either dextrorotatory or levorotatory
It rotates plane-polarized light clockwise
choices.why: D once meant dextrorotatory for glyceraldehyde, but for sugars in general D has no relation to the direction of rotation.

choices.text: It rotates plane-polarized light counterclockwise
choices.why: D says nothing about the direction of rotation.

choices.text: It rotates plane-polarized light by the same amount as D-glyceraldehyde
choices.why: D says nothing about the sign or size of a sugar's rotation.

explanation: The D and L notations have no relation to the direction in which a given sugar rotates plane-polarized light. The prefix D indicates only that the –OH group at the lowest chirality center has R stereochemistry and points to the right in a standard Fischer projection.

choices.text: (2S,3R,4S,5S)-2,3,4,5,6-pentahydroxyhexanal
(2R,3S,4R,5S)-2,3,4,5,6-pentahydroxyhexanal
choices.why: Changing only carbon 5 gives a different sugar, not the mirror image. An L sugar has the opposite configuration at all chirality centers.

choices.text: (2S,3S,4S,5S)-2,3,4,5,6-pentahydroxyhexanal
choices.why: Each center must be inverted: R becomes S and S becomes R, so carbon 3 becomes R.

choices.text: (2R,3S,4R,5R)-2,3,4,5,6-pentahydroxyhexanal
choices.why: That is D-glucose itself. L-glucose is its mirror image.

explanation: An L sugar is the mirror image (enantiomer) of the corresponding D sugar and has the opposite configuration at all chirality centers. Inverting each center of (2R,3S,4R,5R) gives (2S,3R,4S,5S).

prompt: An aldohexose is known to be a D sugar. What does that tell you about its configurations at carbons 2, 3, and 4?

choices.text: Nothing; D describes only the lowest chirality center
All three have the R configuration, like carbon 5
choices.why: D fixes only the lowest chirality center (carbon 5) as R. The other centers can be R or S.

choices.text: All three have the configuration opposite to carbon 5
choices.why: D says nothing about the other centers; they aren't set relative to carbon 5.

choices.text: Their –OH groups all point to the right in a Fischer projection
choices.why: Only the bottom –OH, at the lowest chirality center, must point to the right.

explanation: The D,L system describes the configuration at only one chirality center, the one farthest from the carbonyl group, and says nothing about the configuration of other chirality centers that may be present.

prompt: D-Xylulose is a ketopentose whose chirality centers are 3S,4R. Which carbon (give its number) decides that it is a D sugar?
explanation: D or L is set by the chirality center farthest from the carbonyl group. In D-xylulose (Exercise 25.3.1), carbon 4 is that center, and its R configuration makes it a D sugar.

prompt: Why do glucose, fructose, and most other naturally occurring monosaccharides have the R configuration of D-glyceraldehyde at the chirality center farthest from the carbonyl group?

choices.text: Because of the way monosaccharides are biosynthesized in nature
Because the R configuration is always the more stable one
choices.why: The section explains it by biosynthesis, not by stability.

choices.text: Because all naturally occurring sugars are dextrorotatory
choices.why: A D sugar can be either dextrorotatory or levorotatory.

choices.text: Because L sugars can't have a chirality center at that position
choices.why: L sugars do have that chirality center; it simply has the S configuration.

explanation: Because of the way that monosaccharides are biosynthesized in nature, glucose, fructose, and most other naturally occurring monosaccharides have the same R configuration as D-glyceraldehyde at the chirality center farthest from the carbonyl group. They are D sugars.

prompt: In a standard Fischer projection of an L sugar, where does the –OH at the lowest chirality center point, and what is that center's configuration?

choices.text: To the left; S
To the right; R
choices.why: That describes a D sugar.

choices.text: To the left; R
choices.why: In L sugars the lowest chirality center is S, with its –OH pointing to the left.

choices.text: To the right; S
choices.why: In a standard Fischer projection, a bottom –OH on the right corresponds to R, as in D sugars.

explanation: L sugars have an S configuration at the lowest chirality center, with the bottom –OH group pointing to the left in Fischer projections. D sugars have R, with that –OH pointing to the right.
